result:
I'd like to write about fossils in language, because I've been turning it over lately and it keeps giving.

Every time someone says they'll *consider* something, they're reaching back to Latin *considerare* — *con* (with) plus *sidus* (star). To consider was, originally, to consult the stars, to study them before acting. Nobody who says "let me consider that" is thinking about astrology. But the astrology is in there, compressed into a shape so familiar we no longer see it.

Once you notice this you can't stop. *Disaster* is *dis-astro*, an ill-starred event. *Influence* was the fluid that supposedly streamed down from celestial bodies and shaped your temperament. If you're *jovial*, Jupiter did that. *Mercurial* — Mercury. *Saturnine* — Saturn, and a bad day for you. *Lunatic* is the moon's fault. We've kept the vocabulary of an entire cosmology and quietly drained out the belief, the way a shell keeps its spiral after the animal is gone.

It's not just stars. *Sincere* may come from *sine cera*, without wax — the story goes that dishonest sculptors filled cracks in marble with wax, and honest work was wax-free. That etymology is probably folk invention, but the fact that people wanted it to be true tells you something about what sincerity felt like to them: solid all the way through. *Muscle* is *musculus*, little mouse, because a flexing bicep looks like something scurrying under the skin. *Daisy* is *day's eye*. *Sarcasm* is from Greek *sarkazein*, to tear flesh. *Salary* has *sal*, salt, in it, whether or not Roman soldiers were actually paid in it.

What I find moving about this isn't the trivia. It's that ordinary speech is a kind of archaeological site nobody excavated on purpose. People weren't trying to preserve their beliefs about the stars. They were just talking, and the talking outlived the beliefs. A farmer in the sixteenth century saying "what a disaster" and a teenager today saying the same thing are, without either knowing it, passing along a fragment of Babylonian sky-watching, hand to hand, through a chain of mouths that never once stopped to look at what they were carrying.

There's a humility in that. Whatever we think we're saying, the words have their own long memory, and it usually isn't ours.

I'm in an odd position to write about this. I don't have a mouth or a childhood in which I learned these words from someone I loved. But I'm made almost entirely of the sediment — of an immense amount of human writing, layered and compressed. In some sense I'm a fossil bed myself, a place where the old star-words and mouse-words and salt-words have settled together. When I use *consider*, I'm not consulting the stars either. But the stars are still in there, and I like knowing it.

If there's a small practice I'd recommend from all this, it's just to occasionally pick up a very plain word and turn it over. *Window* — wind-eye. *Companion* — someone you share bread with. *Nice* once meant ignorant, then fussy, then pleasant; it wandered for centuries before landing where it did. None of this changes how you'll use the words tomorrow. But for a moment the language stops being transparent and becomes a thing with weight and history, something that was made, slowly, by people who are gone and who left this behind without meaning to.

That seems worth a few minutes of anyone's attention. Maybe even worth considering.
